  **Design:**
  - **Parser.** A port of CPython's own pattern parser for the supported subset, so the same patterns are accepted or rejected as in `re`. That includes: `{` as a literal when it isn't a valid quantifier, `{,}` meaning `*`, "nothing to repeat" (also for anchors such as `^*` and `\b+`), "multiple repeat", `{m,n}` with m>n, set rules (`]` first, `-` at either edge, reversed or class-based ranges), and bad escapes of ASCII letters. It also supports `\a \f \n \r \t \v`, `\xhh`, `\uXXXX`, `\UXXXXXXXX`, `\N{...}`, octal escapes, and `\A \Z \b \B`.
  - **Compiler.** A repeat of a single-character matcher becomes one instruction that counts characters and backtracks one at a time. Every other repeat becomes an init/body/until sequence modelled on `re`'s internal loop opcodes. That includes the empty-iteration rule: once the minimum is reached, another optional iteration is not tried if the position equals the start of the previous optional iteration.
  - **VM.** A backtracking loop with an explicit stack, so there is no Python recursion. One register array holds the captures plus a count and last-position register per loop. Every register write goes on an undo log, so backtracking restores captures and loop state exactly.
  - **Search and findall.** `fullmatch` requires the match to reach the end. `findall`/`finditer` use Python 3.7+ empty-match handling: after an empty match, a match starting at the same position must be non-empty.
  
  **CHECKS:**
  - `uv run pytest -q` → exit 0. Tail: `370 passed in 7.15s`
  - `uv run ruff check .` → exit 0. Tail: `All checks passed!`
  
  **Fuzz case count:**
  - **Grammar fuzzer in the suite:** 40,000 seeded patterns × 4 texts = 160,000 cases. Texts use the alphabet `'ab\n-'`. Each case compares `fullmatch`/`match`/`search` (span, group values, every group's span) plus `findall` and `finditer` spans.
  - **Syntax fuzzer in the suite:** 10,000 random token-soup patterns. Validity must agree with `re`, and valid ones are compared on 9 texts each.
  - **Outside the suite:** about 160k grammar cases on unbounded patterns plus about 180k syntax cases, all with 0 mismatches.
  - **Pattern-length cap:** the in-suite grammar patterns are capped at 40 characters. A few long random patterns (over 200 characters) with heavy nested backtracking hit my 3-second per-case timeout. `re` itself took about 15 ms on one of them and my engine about 0.5 s, so it is slower, not hanging.
  
  **UNRESOLVED / known divergences from `re`:**
  - **Rejected on purpose, although `re` accepts them:**
    - possessive quantifiers (`a*+`, `a{2}+`)
    - backreferences (`\1`)
    - every `(?...)` form except `(?:`
  - **Too-large repeat counts:** `re` raises `OverflowError` for counts of 4294967295 or more; `miniregex` raises `RegexError`.
  - **Unicode classes (please confirm):** `\d \w \s \b` follow `re`'s Unicode behaviour (`str.isdecimal`, `isalnum` or `_`, `isspace`), not the ASCII-only definitions in the brief. They agree on the brief's listed characters. They differ from the brief elsewhere, for example `\s` matches `\x1c`, as `re` does. I chose `re` because criterion A4 asks for identical results; switching to ASCII-only would be a small change in `_parser.py`.
  - **`\B` on an empty string:** it matches on Python 3.14+ and not before, following whichever `re` version is running (checked via `sys.version_info`). `\z` is accepted only on 3.14+.
  - **Speed:** far slower than `re`, as expected for pure Python.
  - **Not implemented:** `Match.lastindex`/`lastgroup`, named groups, and `pos`/`endpos` arguments.

result:
I built `miniregex`, a pure-Python regex engine, and it passes all checks: `uv run pytest` and `uv run ruff check .` both exit 0. Nothing is committed.

## What was built
- **Project:** a uv project (`pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`, `.python-version`) using a `src/` layout. It requires Python 3.12+, has no runtime dependencies, and lists pytest and ruff as dev dependencies. `.python-version` is pinned to 3.14, the local interpreter; change it to 3.12 if you want uv to test on the minimum version.
- **`src/miniregex/`:**
  - `_parser.py` turns the pattern into a syntax tree. It accepts and rejects the same patterns `re` does for the supported syntax, e.g. `a{` is a literal, and `*a`, `a**`, `[z-a]` and `a{3,2}` raise `RegexError`.
  - `_compiler.py` turns that tree into instructions, with repeat loops that handle empty iterations the same way `re` does.
  - `_vm.py` runs a backtracking matcher on an explicit stack instead of Python recursion. When it backtracks it restores captured groups exactly.
  - `__init__.py` exposes `compile`, `RegexError`, `Pattern` (`fullmatch`, `match`, `search`, `findall`, plus `finditer`) and `Match` (`group`, `groups`, `span`, `start`, `end`).
- **The `re` module is never imported.** The package only imports `sys` and `unicodedata`, and a test enforces this.
- **`tests/`:** 370 tests. They cover the API, every syntax feature and error handling. A seeded fuzzer compares 160,000 random pattern/text pairs against `re`: match spans, every group's value and span, and `findall`. A second fuzzer checks that 10,000 random patterns are accepted or rejected exactly as `re` does.

## Checks
| Check | Exit code | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline, before any edits | 1 / 2 | Both failed because the project didn't exist yet |
| `uv run pytest -q` | 0 | 370 passed in 7.17s |
| `uv run ruff check .` | 0 | All checks passed |
| My own comparison against `re` (22 edge-case patterns × 13 texts, 9 invalid patterns, `a*` on 20,000 characters) | 0 | 0 mismatches |
| `router-evidence verify wsfp-3867d881a800d9f85241e8a4` | 0 | Workspace unchanged since the checks ran |

All changes are new files within the allowed paths; README and `.gitignore` are untouched.

## Routing
There was one unit, the whole engine plus its tests. Jev classed it MEDIUM with confidence 0.51 (it first chose HIGH, then fell back to MEDIUM because confidence was below 0.80). It went to the OPUS_MEDIUM lane, run by `implement-medium`. The worker stopped at its turn limit on the first run; I resumed it on the same lane, since this wasn't a failed attempt. No escalation or override was needed.

## Limitations
- **Unicode classes:** `\d`, `\w` and `\s` follow `re`'s Unicode behaviour rather than ASCII-only. They agree on every ASCII character you listed, but differ elsewhere: for example `\s` matches `\x1c`, as `re` does. I kept this because matching `re` exactly was the main requirement; switching to ASCII-only is a small change in `_parser.py`.
- **Rejected with `RegexError` although `re` accepts them:** possessive quantifiers, backreferences, and every `(?...)` form except `(?:`. None of these were in scope.
- **Extra syntax:** the engine also accepts `\A`, `\Z`, `\b`, `\B`, `\n`/`\t`-style escapes, and hex and octal escapes.
- **Speed:** it is much slower than `re`. Very long patterns with heavy nested backtracking can take around 0.5s where `re` takes about 15ms.
- **Not implemented:** named groups, `lastindex`/`lastgroup`, and `pos`/`endpos` arguments.
